maintenance: Party lanes need a two-line edit every other January after a new Congress is seated (next: January 2027). Fed chair, FOMC estimates and events are edited as they happen.
political_note: Control is shown as of inauguration (January 20) and the seating of each Congress (January 3). Policy acts with a lag, often a year or more, and shocks do not follow the election calendar.

overlays.label: Fed's 2% inflation target
overlays.note: The target is set on PCE inflation, which usually runs a few tenths below the CPI shown here. Turn on the PCE companion to see the index the target actually applies to.

overlays.label: FOMC longer-run Fed funds estimate (3.2%)
overlays.note: Median of FOMC participants' estimates of the rate consistent with full employment and 2% inflation, from the September 2026 projections. An estimate, revised quarterly.

overlays.label: FOMC longer-run unemployment estimate (4.2%)
overlays.note: Median FOMC estimate of the unemployment rate consistent with stable inflation, September 2026 projections. Compare the CBO's estimate under companion series.

overlays.label: CBO projection for 2056 (175%)
overlays.note: Where the Congressional Budget Office projects debt held by the public under current law. A projection, revised each year; the 2025 record was 99%.

source.label: CBO, The Long-Term Budget Outlook: 2026 to 2056

overlays.label: 1946 peak (106%)
overlays.note: Debt held by the public at the end of World War II, the previous record, as a share of GDP. The chart's own series starts in 1970.

overlays.label: Sahm rule threshold (0.5)
overlays.note: Applies to the Sahm indicator, not the unemployment rate itself. Shown only when that companion is on.

overlays.label: 2015–19 average
overlays.note: The last five full years before the pandemic. A stand-in for recent normal, not a target.

overlays.label: Median since records began
overlays.note: Half of all readings are above this line, half below.

overlays.label: Party of the president
overlays.note: Control is shown as of inauguration (January 20) and the seating of each Congress (January 3). Policy acts with a lag, often a year or more, and shocks do not follow the election calendar.

overlays.label: Senate majority
overlays.note: Control is shown as of inauguration (January 20) and the seating of each Congress (January 3). Policy acts with a lag, often a year or more, and shocks do not follow the election calendar. The Senate changed hands three times within the 2001–03 Congress; see the lane.

overlays.label: House majority
overlays.note: Control is shown as of inauguration (January 20) and the seating of each Congress (January 3). Policy acts with a lag, often a year or more, and shocks do not follow the election calendar.

overlays.label: Unified or divided government
overlays.note: Control is shown as of inauguration (January 20) and the seating of each Congress (January 3). Policy acts with a lag, often a year or more, and shocks do not follow the election calendar. Unified means one party holds the presidency and both chambers.

overlays.label: Federal Reserve chair
overlays.note: Monetary policy is set by a 12-member committee, not the chair alone, and its effects take a year or more to show.

overlays.label: Fed bond-buying (QE) and runoff
overlays.note: Periods when the Fed was expanding its holdings of Treasuries and mortgage bonds (QE) or letting them shrink. Dates are the announced start and end of net purchases or runoff.

overlays.label: Fed rate hikes and cuts
overlays.note: From the first change in the Fed funds target in one direction to the last, two or more moves. Before 1988 the Fed did not announce a target and moved it in frequent small steps; those years are left blank.

segments.label: Hikes
segments.note: 1.00% to 5.25%, a quarter point at 17 straight meetings

segments.label: Hikes
segments.note: 0–0.25% to 5.25–5.50%, the fastest since the early 1980s

source.label: Federal Reserve Board, Open Market Operations

overlays.label: U.S. at war
overlays.note: Rule: declared wars and conflicts Congress authorized, from the authorization to the end of U.S. combat, plus Korea, fought under a UN resolution. Conflicts without an authorization (Kosovo, Libya, the 2026 strikes on Iran) are not shown here; those that moved an indicator are under Shocks and crises.

segments.label: World War II
segments.note: Declaration of war to the Japanese surrender.

segments.label: Korea
segments.note: U.S. forces committed under a UN resolution; never declared or authorized by Congress. Ends at the armistice.

segments.label: Vietnam
segments.note: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution to the withdrawal of the last U.S. combat troops.

segments.label: Afghanistan
segments.note: 2001 authorization to the completion of the withdrawal.

segments.label: Afghanistan & Iraq
segments.note: Afghanistan: 2001 authorization to the completion of the withdrawal. Iraq: 2002 authorization (combat began March 2003) to the departure of the last U.S. troops.

segments.label: Afghanistan
segments.note: 2001 authorization to the completion of the withdrawal.

source.label: Congressional Research Service, Declarations of War and Authorizations

overlays.label: Shocks and crises
overlays.note: An event is listed if it visibly moved at least one indicator on this site within three months, or committed federal money or changed federal policy on a scale that shows up in GDP investment, household income or an indicator here over the following years. Nothing is listed because it fits a story. Dates are when the thing happened or was signed, not when its effects showed up.

items.label: Oil embargo
items.note: OPEC embargo begins; oil prices quadruple over the following months.

items.label: Second oil shock
items.note: The Shah leaves Iran; oil output collapses and prices more than double.

items.label: Plaza Accord
items.note: Five governments agree to push the dollar down.

items.label: Black Monday
items.note: Stocks fall 22% in a day.

items.label: Iraq invades Kuwait
items.note: Oil doubles within two months; the recession is dated from July.

items.label: Dot-com peak
items.note: The Nasdaq's high; it loses three-quarters of its value over the next two years.

items.label: Hurricane Katrina
items.note: Jobless claims and energy prices jump in the weeks after.

items.label: Lehman Brothers fails
items.note: The largest bankruptcy in U.S. history; credit markets seize.

items.label: Taper tantrum
items.note: Bond yields jump after the Fed signals the end of QE3 purchases.

items.label: COVID national emergency
items.note: Declared March 13; the WHO had called it a pandemic on the 11th.

items.label: Russia invades Ukraine
items.note: Oil passes $120 and U.S. gasoline tops $5 by June; wheat and fertilizer prices jump.

items.label: Silicon Valley Bank fails
items.note: Second-largest bank failure in U.S. history at the time.

items.label: U.S. and Israel strike Iran
items.note: Iran closes the Strait of Hormuz to most shipping within days; gasoline is up a third over the following months. No congressional authorization, so not shown on the war lane.

overlays.label: Major tax and spending laws
overlays.note: Date signed. An event is listed if it visibly moved at least one indicator on this site within three months, or committed federal money or changed federal policy on a scale that shows up in GDP investment, household income or an indicator here over the following years. Nothing is listed because it fits a story. Dates are when the thing happened or was signed, not when its effects showed up.

items.label: Tax Reform Act of 1986
items.note: Lowers rates, broadens the base.

items.label: TARP
items.note: $700 billion bank rescue signed.

items.label: Recovery Act (ARRA)
items.note: $787 billion stimulus signed.

items.label: Sequestration
items.note: Across-the-board federal spending cuts begin.

items.label: CARES Act
items.note: $2.2 trillion pandemic relief signed.

items.label: Second pandemic relief bill
items.note: $900 billion, including $600 payments, in the year-end appropriations act.

items.label: American Rescue Plan
items.note: $1.9 trillion pandemic relief signed.

items.label: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
items.note: $1.2 trillion over several years for roads, transit, broadband, water and the grid.

items.label: CHIPS and Science Act
items.note: $52 billion in grants and a 25% tax credit for semiconductor plants.

items.label: Inflation Reduction Act
items.note: Energy and manufacturing tax credits, drug-price negotiation, a corporate minimum tax.

items.label: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
items.note: Extends the 2017 tax cuts and changes spending programs.

Fed cuts to zero

items.label: First hike since 2023

items.label: Steel and aluminum tariffs
items.note: Section 232 tariffs; broader China tariffs follow in July.

items.label: Broad tariffs announced
items.note: 'Liberation Day' tariffs on most trading partners.

items.label: Supreme Court strikes down IEEPA tariffs

overlays.label: Government shutdowns (2 weeks or longer)
overlays.note: Start dates. Shorter funding lapses, of which there have been several, are not shown.

items.label: Shutdown, 21 days
items.note: Through January 6, 1996.

items.label: Shutdown, 16 days
items.note: Through October 17, 2013.

items.label: Shutdown, 35 days
items.note: Through January 25, 2019. Partial.

items.label: Shutdown, 43 days
items.note: Through November 12, 2025. The longest on record; October's jobs and CPI reports were delayed or skipped.

overlays.label: Federal minimum wage increases
overlays.note: Effective dates of each increase in the federal minimum. Many states set higher minimums, so the federal rate has bound less and less of the workforce since the 1980s.
